body.text: Associated corporations in Canada must share one SR&ED expenditure limit under the Income Tax Act. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, associated Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) allocate a single $6,000,000 limit for the enhanced 35% investment tax credit on Schedule T2SCH49, and their combined prior-year taxable capital drives the $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 phase-out.

Canada operates one of the world's most comprehensive fiscal frameworks for business innovation, anchored federally by the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program under the Income Tax Act (ITA), R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) and the Income Tax Regulations (ITR), C.R.C., c. 945. Between June 2024 and November 2026, the Canadian research and development (R&D) tax landscape underwent its most substantial legislative transformation since 2012 through three successive federal milestones: the enactment of Bill C-69 (Budget Implementation Act, 2024, No. 1) on June 20, 2024, which retroactively exempted bona fide concessional government loans from reducing SR&ED expenditure pools; the Royal Assent of Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1) on March 26, 2026, which doubled the enhanced 35% refundable investment tax credit (ITC) expenditure limit to $6,000,000, widened the taxable capital phase-out thresholds to $15,000,000–$75,000,000, extended the 35% refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), and reinstated the eligibility of capital expenditures and equipment lease costs after December 15, 2024; and the tabling of Federal Budget 2026 on November 5, 2026, which proposed expanding SR&ED to include regulatory certification testing and intellectual property (IP) protection costs for taxation years beginning after November 4, 2026. Concurrently, at the provincial level, Québec replaced its legacy R&D tax credits with the unified, fully refundable 30%/20% Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, while British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Ontario, Alberta, Manitoba, and the Atlantic provinces established distinct alignment postures toward the federal Bill C-15 reforms.
1. Executive Summary and Macro-Fiscal Architecture
1.1 Scale and Policy Mandate of the SR&ED Program

The SR&ED Tax Incentive Program is the primary pillar of Canadian industrial and technological policy, delivering non-dilutive financial support to businesses conducting systematic investigation or search in fields of science or technology within Canada. Administered jointly by the Department of Finance Canada, which formulates statutory tax policy, and the Canada Revenue Agency, which executes technical eligibility reviews, financial audits, and tax credit assessments, the program has expanded significantly over the past five fiscal cycles. According to CRA program statistics cited in industry analyses, in fiscal year 2024–2025 the CRA processed 22,758 SR&ED claims across more than 19,000 claimants, delivering $4.5 billion in federal investment tax credits. For the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026, industry reporting of CRA data indicates that total federal SR&ED ITCs claimed reached $4.9 billion, with $4.6 billion allowed—an increase of roughly 50% in annual credit value since fiscal year 2022. Furthermore, the Department of Finance's 2026 Spring Economic Update projects that recent enhancements to the SR&ED tax incentives will generate an additional $1.2 billion per year in national economic output.
1.2 The Dual-Pillar Statutory Incentive Mechanism

Under the federal Income Tax Act, the SR&ED program operates through a synchronized two-step statutory mechanism that separates the income tax deductibility of R&D outlays from the calculation and refund of investment tax credits.

First, under Section 37 of the ITA (Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures), subsection 37(1) permits a taxpayer to pool allowable current expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(a) and, for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, allowable capital expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(b) incurred for SR&ED carried on in Canada. Rather than being restricted to annual Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) depreciation schedules, the balance in the subsection 37(1) pool may be deducted in whole or in part to reduce net business income for tax purposes in the current taxation year, or carried forward indefinitely to offset business income in any subsequent taxation year.

Second, under Sections 127 and 127.1 of the ITA (SR&ED Investment Tax Credits), subsections 127(5) and 127(9) to (10.8) and section 127.1 enable a claimant to earn an Investment Tax Credit (ITC) calculated as a specified percentage—either the 15% basic rate or the 35% enhanced rate—of its year-end "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool". Depending on the legal status of the claimant and whether the underlying expenditure is current or capital in nature, the earned ITC is applied to reduce federal Part I tax otherwise payable, refunded directly in cash at 100% or 40% refundability rates, or carried back 3 taxation years and carried forward up to 20 taxation years.

body.text: 2. Statutory Definition of SR&ED and Technical Eligibility Criteria
2.1 Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act

Whether a project qualifies for federal and provincial R&D incentives in Canada is governed by the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. Neither Bill C-15 nor Bill C-69 altered the core wording of subsection 248(1), which conforms broadly to the OECD Frascati Manual while imposing specific statutory inclusions and exclusions.

Under the preamble of subsection 248(1), "scientific research and experimental development" means a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis and that falls within one of three core categories, supplemented by a fourth category of directly supporting work and delimited by seven statutory exclusions:

items: Paragraph (a) — Basic Research: Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view.
Paragraph (b) — Applied Research: Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view.

Paragraph (c) — Experimental Development: Work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto.

Paragraph (d) — Directly Supporting Work: In applying the definition in respect of a taxpayer, SR&ED includes work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, where the work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of work described in paragraph (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer.

Paragraphs (e) to (k) — Statutory Exclusions: Subsection 248(1) explicitly excludes any work with respect to: (e) market research or sales promotion; (f) quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; (g) research in the social sciences or the humanities; (h) prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; (i) the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process; (j) style changes; or (k) routine data collection.

body.text: 2.2 Evolution of Administrative Doctrine: From IC 86-4R3 and the Five Questions to the "Why" and "How" Framework

The administrative interpretation of subsection 248(1) has evolved through three major doctrinal stages. Prior to 1985, Revenue Canada relied on Interpretation Bulletin IT-439, which taxpayers and the Department of Finance recognized as insufficient to define eligible development work. Following the May 1985 federal budget—which introduced the term "experimental development" into the Regulations to exclude routine engineering—and a March 4, 1986 policy clarification from the Department of Finance, Revenue Canada partnered with industry specialists to issue Information Circular IC 86-4, revised in 1994 as IC 86-4R3 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development). IC 86-4R3 established three foundational criteria for SR&ED eligibility: scientific or technological advancement, scientific or technological uncertainty, and scientific and technical content through systematic investigation.

In 1998, Judge Bowman of the Tax Court of Canada synthesized IC 86-4R3 and subsection 248(1) in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen (98 D.T.C. 1839) into a five-question judicial test. The CRA subsequently adopted those five questions as the structural backbone of its Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy (published in 2012 and revised in 2015). Under that framework, reviewers evaluated: (1) whether there was a scientific or technological uncertainty; (2) whether the effort involved formulating hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that uncertainty; (3) whether the overall approach adopted was consistent with a systematic investigation or search, including formulating and testing the hypotheses by means of experiment or analysis; (4) whether the overall approach was undertaken for the purpose of achieving a scientific or technological advancement; and (5) whether a record of the hypotheses tested and the results was kept as the work progressed.

On August 13, 2021, following a 2020 modernization review, the CRA archived the 2015 policy document and published the Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives. While the Tax Court of Canada and Federal Court of Appeal continue to enforce the five Northwest Hydraulic questions as binding judicial precedent, the CRA's current administrative guidelines streamline those five questions into two overarching requirements derived directly from subsection 248(1): the "Why" requirement and the "How" requirement.

cells: "...for the advancement of scientific knowledge..." or "...for the purpose of achieving technological advancement..."

The work must seek to generate or discover new scientific or technological knowledge by resolving a scientific or technological uncertainty that cannot be removed by standard practice, routine engineering, or knowledge available to competent professionals in the field.
"systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis"

The work must follow a structured scientific methodology: (1) formulating an idea/hypothesis consistent with known facts; (2) testing the hypothesis via experiment or analysis; (3) drawing logical conclusions from results; and (4) keeping contemporaneous records as work progresses.

body.text: 2.3 Deep-Dive Analysis of the "Why" and "How" Requirements

To satisfy the "Why" requirement, a claimant must establish that existing scientific or technological knowledge was insufficient to achieve the desired objective, creating a genuine scientific or technological uncertainty whose resolution is sought to achieve a scientific or technological advancement. Under the CRA guidelines and Tax Court jurisprudence (such as Airzone One Ltd. v. The Queen, JEC Distributors Inc. v. The King, and Mold Leaders Inc. v. The King), the baseline of available knowledge is an objective industry standard measured against competent professionals in the relevant field of science or technology, combined with the knowledge resources available within the claimant's business—not merely the subjective unfamiliarity of the claimant's own staff. Acquiring available knowledge or know-how through literature searches, training, on-the-job learning, hiring expert employees or consultants, purchasing proprietary knowledge, or adopting a "workaround" that bypasses the technical barrier using known methods does not satisfy the requirement of attempting to achieve a technological advancement.

Both the CRA's Guidelines on the eligibility of work for SR&ED tax incentives and the Tax Court in Airzone One Ltd. identify seven specific diagnostic indicators that suggest existing technological knowledge is insufficient:

items: Existing design methods or established engineering procedures are not applicable.
Performance requirements or technical specifications do not conform to existing industry standards.
There are too many variables or unknown interactions to predict the outcome ("system uncertainty").
Operating parameters or environmental conditions lie outside the normal operating range.
The nature of the technical problem is evolving dynamically as investigation proceeds.
Required empirical data is not readily available in public literature or technical specifications.
Interlocking technical constraints exist where resolving one parameter degrades another in ways standard trade-off calculations cannot predict.

body.text: Importantly, achieving commercial novelty, innovation, uniqueness, feature enhancement, or increased product functionality does not in itself demonstrate scientific or technological advancement. Conversely, a project that fails to achieve its commercial or technical goals still qualifies for SR&ED if it satisfies the "Why" and "How" requirements. As established in Rainbow Pipe Line Co. v. The Queen, the conclusive rejection of a hypothesis through systematic testing is itself a technological advancement because it generates new knowledge by eliminating a plausible technological option.

To satisfy the "How" requirement, the claimant must demonstrate that the investigation was conducted systematically by qualified personnel rather than through trial-and-error or routine debugging. The CRA guidelines specify four sequential elements for the "How" requirement: (1) generating an idea or hypothesis consistent with known facts that serves as a starting point for investigation; (2) testing that idea or hypothesis by means of experiment or analysis, allowing the hypothesis to evolve as testing progresses; (3) developing logical conclusions based on the empirical results or findings of the experiment or analysis; and (4) keeping contemporaneous evidence generated as the work progresses.
2.4 Distinguishing Support Work from Excluded Work and Company Projects

A frequent source of audit disallowances is conflating a "company project"—a commercial undertaking such as developing a new product line, expanding a facility, or upgrading commercial software—with an "SR&ED project," which comprises only the interrelated activities necessary to resolve scientific or technological uncertainties through experiment or analysis. Claimants must identify SR&ED projects at the level where all captured effort falls within subsection 248(1), rather than subdividing an eligible project into isolated tasks that appear routine out of context, or sweeping commercial production tasks into the R&D claim.

Once core basic research, applied research, or experimental development is established, work in the eight exclusive support categories of paragraph 248(1)(d)—engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research—qualifies only if it is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of the core SR&ED work undertaken in Canada. As the CRA guidelines explain, the key feature distinguishing eligible support work under paragraph (d) from excluded work under paragraphs (e) to (k) is purpose. If data collection or testing is carried out for routine quality control or market research, it is statutorily excluded under paragraphs 248(1)(e), (f), or (k); if the exact same physical testing or data collection is carried out specifically to evaluate an experimental hypothesis in support of core SR&ED, it qualifies under paragraph 248(1)(d). Furthermore, SR&ED eligibility ceases on the project completion date, defined in the T661 Guide (T4088) as the earliest point at which the claimant: (1) achieved the scientific or technological advancement by resolving the associated uncertainties; (2) determined that the uncertainties cannot be resolved; or (3) terminated the project for any reason.
2.5 Proposed Budget 2026 Expansion: Regulatory Certification and IP Protection Costs

Historically, once a claimant resolved the technological uncertainty of an SR&ED project, downstream regulatory certification testing and intellectual property registration fees were excluded from SR&ED as post-development commercial expenses or prescribed legal fees under ITR section 2902. In Federal Budget 2026 (tabled November 5, 2026), the Department of Finance proposed expanding the SR&ED program for taxation years that begin after November 4, 2026 (on or after Budget Day, November 5, 2026) across two new areas:

First, under the Regulatory and Certification Requirements expansion, eligible SR&ED activities are proposed to include tests, technological validations, and studies conducted to meet regulatory requirements to obtain the initial approval or certification necessary to commercialize a product or process, provided these activities directly relate to a project that is eligible under the existing rules of the SR&ED program. Standard SR&ED expenditure categories—including wages and salaries, materials, contracting costs, overhead costs, and machinery and equipment—will be claimable for these regulatory activities.

Second, under the Intellectual Property (IP) Protection Costs expansion, eligible SR&ED expenditures are proposed to cover costs reasonably incurred for the registration and maintenance of IP protection for IP developed during an eligible SR&ED project. Eligible forms of IP encompass patents, certificates of supplementary protection, plant breeders' rights, and copyrighted software registered or protected under relevant Canadian legislation or equivalent foreign legislation. Claimable IP costs include preparing and filing IP protection applications and paying periodic maintenance fees to keep IP rights in force. While administrative fees paid to an IP office outside Canada will qualify, the costs of supporting activities—such as preparing a patent application—will qualify only if those activities are conducted in Canada. Costs incurred to enforce IP rights (such as patent infringement litigation) remain excluded, and recapture rules will apply to claw back the related SR&ED deduction and ITC if the taxpayer subsequently disposes of the IP.
3. Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures and Foreign R&D Rules
3.1 Mechanics of the Subsection 37(1) Deductible Expenditure Pool

Subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act establishes a running, cumulative tax account—the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures—calculated in Part 3, Section C of Form T661. Unlike ordinary capital expenses subject to annual Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) depreciation limits under paragraph 20(1)(a) and Part XI of the Regulations, expenditures added to the subsection 37(1) pool may be deducted in full or in part in the current taxation year, or carried forward indefinitely to offset business income in any subsequent taxation year.

body.text: 3.2 Negative Pool Balances, Acquisition of Rights, and Partnership Rules
Three technical rules in the CRA's Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures Policy govern special adjustments to the subsection 37(1) pool:

First, under the Negative Pool Balance Rule (Paragraph 12(1)(v) and Paragraph 37(1)(c.1)), because federal SR&ED ITCs claimed or refunded in a taxation year reduce the subsection 37(1) pool in the following taxation year under paragraph 37(1)(e), a claimant that deducts its entire subsection 37(1) pool in Year 1 and incurs zero SR&ED expenditures in Year 2 will have a negative pool balance at the end of Year 2. The opening balance of the pool at the start of a taxation year cannot be negative. Any negative balance at the end of a taxation year must be included in net business income for tax purposes in that year under paragraph 12(1)(v), and an equivalent amount is added to the pool in the subsequent year under paragraph 37(1)(c.1) to reset the opening pool balance to nil.

Second, under the Prohibition on Acquiring Rights (Subsection 37(4)), no deduction is allowed under subsection 37(1) for an expenditure made to acquire rights in, or arising out of, SR&ED—such as buying an existing patent or paying a separate sum at the end of a contract to purchase IP owned by the contractor. The CRA's policy explains that allowing the purchaser of rights to claim SR&ED incentives would either duplicate the tax incentive already available to the performer or improperly subsidize R&D performed outside Canada.

Third, under the Partnership Carryforward Prohibition, a partnership cannot carry forward an undeducted balance in the subsection 37(1) pool to a subsequent fiscal period. The entire pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures of a partnership must be deducted in full when computing the partnership's net business income in the fiscal period in which the expenditures were incurred.
3.3 SR&ED Carried On Outside Canada (Subsections 37(1.3), 37(1.4), 37(1.5), and 37(2))

As a general statutory principle, only SR&ED carried on physically inside Canada—which under subsection 37(1.3) includes Canada's Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) at sea, enacted after LGL Ltd. v. The Queen, 96-4726(IT)G—enters the subsection 37(1) pool and earns ITCs. However, Section 37 provides two specific mechanisms for R&D work performed outside Canada:

First, under Subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) (Permissible Salary or Wages for SR&ED Outside Canada — The 10% Limit), a claimant may include salary or wages paid to Canadian-resident employees for SR&ED work carried on outside Canada (reported on Form T661 Line 307 for regular employees and Line 309 for specified employees) in both the subsection 37(1) pool and the qualified expenditure pool for ITCs, provided all five statutory requirements are met: (1) the work was carried on outside Canada directly by an employee of the taxpayer (work by foreign contractors never qualifies under this rule); (2) the employee was a resident of Canada at the time the expense was incurred; (3) the work related to a business of the taxpayer; (4) the work was integral to and solely in support of core SR&ED carried on in Canada by the taxpayer; and (5) the taxpayer reasonably believes that the salary or wages are not subject to an income or profits tax imposed by a foreign country because of the employee's presence or activity in that country. Under paragraph 37(1.5)(b) ("Limit B" on Form T661), the total permissible foreign SR&ED salary or wages claimed in a taxation year cannot exceed 10% of the total allowable SR&ED salary or wages incurred in the year for SR&ED carried on in Canada.

Second, under Subsection 37(2) (Research Outside Canada — Current Deduction Only), any current expenditures made by a taxpayer on SR&ED carried on outside Canada that do not qualify under subsection 37(1.5)—such as payments to foreign subcontractors performing R&D outside Canada or employee salaries exceeding the 10% cap—may be deducted against current-year business income under subsection 37(2). However, subsection 37(2) expenditures cannot be claimed on Form T661, do not enter the subsection 37(1) pool for indefinite carryforward, and earn 0% ITC.
4. Federal Investment Tax Credit (ITC) Rates, Thresholds, Refundability, and Carryovers
4.1 The Two-Tier Federal ITC Rate Structure and Bill C-15 Expansion
Under subsection 127(9) and subsection 127(10.1) of the Income Tax Act, federal SR&ED ITCs are calculated on a claimant's year-end SR&ED qualified expenditure pool across two rate tiers:

The Basic ITC Rate (15%) is defined under "specified percentage" in subsection 127(9) as 15% (reduced from 20% after 2013). This rate applies to all qualified expenditures of corporations that are neither CCPCs nor ECPCs (such as foreign-controlled subsidiaries and large public corporations), individuals, trusts, and members of partnerships, as well as to qualified expenditures of CCPCs and ECPCs that exceed their annual expenditure limit.

The Enhanced ITC Rate (35%) is established under subsection 127(10.1) by adding a 20% enhancement to the 15% basic rate, creating a combined 35% ITC rate on qualified expenditures up to the corporation's annual Expenditure Limit. For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the 35% enhanced rate applied exclusively to Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) up to a maximum annual expenditure limit of $3,000,000, yielding a maximum annual enhanced ITC of $1,050,000. Under Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026), for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Parliament doubled the annual expenditure limit to $6,000,000—surpassing the $4,500,000 figure originally proposed in the December 16, 2024 Fall Economic Statement and August 15, 2025 draft legislation—and extended eligibility for the 35% enhanced rate to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) alongside CCPCs. Consequently, a qualifying CCPC or ECPC can earn up to $2,100,000 per year in enhanced 35% ITCs.
4.2 Mathematical Phase-Out Formulas for the Annual Expenditure Limit

The annual expenditure limit ($3,000,000 for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024; $6,000,000 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024) must be shared across all associated CCPCs under subsection 127(10.21) using Schedule T2SCH49, or across all members of a consolidated ECPC group preparing consolidated financial statements. Under subsection 127(10.2), the expenditure limit is phased out for medium-to-large corporate groups based on prior-year size metrics:

For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, a CCPC's $3,000,000 expenditure limit begins to decrease linearly once prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada (combined across all associated corporations) reaches $10,000,000, and is reduced to nil at $50,000,000:
Expenditure Limit = $3,000,000 × ($40,000,000 − A) ÷ $40,000,000, where A = prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada in excess of $10,000,000

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, under the Standard CCPC Taxable Capital Method enacted by Bill C-15, the prior-year taxable capital phase-out window was widened to $15,000,000 to $75,000,000:
Expenditure Limit = $6,000,000 × ($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000, where A = prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada in excess of $15,000,000

Alternatively, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 introduced the Average Annual Revenue Method, which is mandatory for Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) and elective for CCPCs. Under this rule, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit decreases linearly between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000 based on the corporation's (or associated/consolidated group's) average annual revenue over the 3 preceding fiscal years as reflected in its financial statements (regardless of whether group members were associated during the entirety of that 3-year period, with reasonable adjustments allowed for intra-group sales of goods or services so the group is measured as a single economic entity):
Expenditure Limit = $6,000,000 × ($60,000,000 − B) ÷ $60,000,000, where B = average annual revenue over the 3 preceding fiscal years in excess of $15,000,000

body.text: Under the CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, SR&ED ITC refunds cannot be claimed in respect of repayments of government or non-government assistance or contract payments (which earn non-refundable ITCs at the historical rate under subsection 127(10.7)), and no ITC is earned if any of the claimant's income from the business is exempt from Part I tax.
4.4 Application, Carryback, Carryforward, and Loss Restriction Rules
When a claimant earns an SR&ED ITC in a taxation year, the credit is administered in four statutory steps:

items: Offset Against Current-Year Part I Tax (Subsection 127(5)): The claimant may apply available ITCs to reduce federal Part I tax otherwise payable in the current taxation year to nil. Per Ainsworth Lumber Co. v. The Queen (98-1052-IT-G, 2001 TCC), because subsection 127(5) states that a taxpayer "may" deduct credits, a taxpayer holding both refundable and non-refundable ITCs may elect the order of deduction to maximize cash refunds.

Cash Refund and Deemed Deduction (Section 127.1 and Subsection 127.1(3)): Any remaining current-year refundable ITC is paid out as a cash refund. Under subsection 127.1(3), any SR&ED ITC refunded to the taxpayer in the year is deemed to have been deducted under subsection 127(5) against Part I tax otherwise payable, which reduces the ITCs available for carryback or carryforward and triggers the paragraph 37(1)(e) pool reduction (or taxable income inclusion) in the following taxation year.

Carryback and Carryforward Periods: Unused SR&ED ITCs may be carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years or carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years (for 2008 and later taxation years) to reduce Part I tax otherwise payable in those years.

Acquisition of Control Restrictions: Under the CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, if a corporation undergoes an acquisition of control, the amount of unused ITCs earned before the acquisition of control that may be carried forward to subsequent years is restricted, and the amount of unused ITCs earned after the acquisition of control that may be carried back to pre-acquisition years is similarly restricted.

body.text: 5. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs) and Methodological Mechanics
5.1 Traditional Method vs. Proxy Method (Clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) vs. Clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B))

When filing Form T661 for a taxation year, a claimant must elect on Line 160 (Proxy Method) or Line 162 (Traditional Method) how it will calculate its SR&ED overhead and indirect support expenditures. body.text: Worked Break-Even Comparison (CRA Benchmark Example: Acme Ltd.)

In Section 6.0 of the CRA's Traditional and Proxy Methods Policy, the CRA illustrates the quantitative trade-off between the two methods using "Acme Ltd.," a CCPC eligible for the 35% ITC that incurs $100,000 in salaries of employees directly engaged in SR&ED, $15,000 in materials for SR&ED, and $50,000 in verifiable incremental overhead expenditures.

Under the Traditional Method, Acme Ltd. adds all three actual outlays ($100,000 + $15,000 + $50,000 = $165,000) to both the subsection 37(1) deductible pool and the qualified SR&ED expenditure pool, earning a 35% ITC of $57,750 ($165,000 × 35%). Under the Proxy Method, Acme Ltd. adds only $115,000 ($100,000 salaries + $15,000 materials) to its subsection 37(1) pool, while deducting the $50,000 of actual overhead as an ordinary business expense under section 9 of the ITA. In Part 5 of Form T661, however, Acme Ltd. computes a Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) of $55,000 ($100,000 salary base × 55% under ITR subsection 2900(4), subject to the overall PPA cap under ITR subsection 2900(6)), raising its total qualified SR&ED expenditures to $170,000 ($115,000 + $55,000) and earning a 35% ITC of $59,500—an additional $1,750 in refundable tax credits without the administrative burden of tracking and defending itemized overhead. Unless provable directly related and incremental overhead exceeds 55% of the eligible salary base, the Proxy Method generates the larger ITC.

Under the Traditional Method, claimants should also note specific CRA inclusions and exclusions in the SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy: moving expenses to relocate SR&ED candidates or employees within Canada (and related employee housing-loss taxable benefits) qualify if directly related and incremental, whereas headhunter fees, recruitment advertising, interview travel, immigration/work-permit costs, fixed-cost maintenance contracts that do not vary with SR&ED usage, post-project waste disposal, SR&ED claim preparation fees, convention/conference fees, and interest expenses are disallowed or prescribed expenditures.
5.2 Salaries and Wages, Specified Employee Caps, and the 180-Day Unpaid Rule

Under subsection 248(1) of the ITA and the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy (updated January 28, 2025), eligible salary or wages consist of income from an office or employment as computed under subdivision a of Division B of Part I (reported on T4 slips) for employees performing hands-on SR&ED tasks, technical planning, technical feasibility studies, internal technical documentation, or first-line technical supervision. Work beyond the first-line level of technical supervision, non-technological management activities, stock option benefits (disallowed for options granted or shares issued on or after November 17, 2005, following Alcatel Canada Inc. v. The Queen, 2005 TCC 149), extended vacation or sick leave, retiring allowances, and shareholder dividends are excluded from SR&ED salary or wages. In addition, under subsection 248(16), any GST/HST or provincial sales tax input tax credit claimed on employee taxable benefits is deemed to be government assistance and must be excluded from allowable SR&ED wages.
Restrictions on "Specified Employees" (Owner-Managers and ≥10% Shareholders)

A "specified employee" is defined in subsection 248(1) of the ITA as an employee who does not deal at arm's length with the employer OR who is a "specified shareholder" owning, directly or indirectly at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or any related corporation. Specified employees are subject to three strict statutory limitations:

First, under Subsection 37(9) of the ITA and Subsection 2900(9) of the ITR, all bonuses and remuneration based on profits paid to a specified employee are completely disallowed from SR&ED salary or wages on Form T661 Line 305 and excluded from the PPA salary base. (Exception: Under Section 6.0 of the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, if an employee directly performs SR&ED duties and their only remuneration in the year consists of bonuses or profit-based remuneration, the CRA considers an amount commensurate with performance to be salary or wages. By contrast, enforceable bonuses paid to regular [non-specified] employees are allowable as SR&ED wages on Line 300, though they must still be subtracted on Line 812 when computing the PPA salary base in Part 5 under ITR subsection 2900(9).)

Second, under Subsections 37(9.1) to 37(9.5) of the ITA (The 5× YMPE Cap on Line 305), the maximum allowable SR&ED salary or wages that a claimant (or group of associated corporations combined) can claim on Form T661 Line 305 for a specified employee is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the year that the individual is a specified employee:
Specified Employee SR&ED Salary Cap (Line 305) = 5 × YMPE × (Days as Specified Employee in Tax Year ÷ 365)

If a specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations, no expenditures may be claimed by any of those corporations unless they file Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for SR&ED) to allocate the 5× YMPE limit among the group.

Third, under Subsections 2900(7) and 2900(8) of the ITR (The Specified Employee PPA Salary Base Cap in Part 5, Lines 850–858), the amount included in the salary base to compute the 55% PPA for each specified employee is restricted to the least of three amounts: (1) the specified employee's eligible SR&ED salary claimed on Line 305 (Line 852 total salary excluding bonuses/taxable benefits/prior-year unpaid wages × Line 854 % of time spent on SR&ED = Line 856); (2) 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages (SR&ED and non-SR&ED combined, excluding bonuses, remuneration based on profits, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year); or (3) 2.5 × YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year that the claimant employed the individual (Line 858, shared across associated corporations under ITR subsection 2900(8)):
Specified Employee PPA Ceiling (Line 858) = 2.5 × YMPE × (Days Employed in Tax Year ÷ 365)

Thus, the owner-manager adds $150,000 to the $300,000 non-specified salary base for a total PPA salary base of $450,000, generating a 55% PPA of $247,500, total qualified expenditures of $737,500 ($300,000 + $160,000 + $30,000 + $247,500), and a 35% federal ITC of $258,125.
The 180-Day Unpaid Remuneration and Unpaid Amounts Rules (Subsections 78(4) and 127(26))

Under subsection 78(4) of the ITA, employee remuneration incurred in a taxation year that is not paid within 180 days after the end of that taxation year is deemed not to have been incurred in that year. Unpaid wages must be identified on Form T661 Line 315 in the year incurred and can only be claimed on Line 310 in the subsequent taxation year in which they are actually paid (and even then, Line 310 amounts are permanently excluded from the Part 5 PPA salary base). Similarly, under subsection 127(26), current SR&ED expenditures other than salary or wages (such as subcontractor invoices or material bills) that remain unpaid 180 days after year-end must be deducted from qualified expenditures on Line 520 and added back only in the year paid (with unpaid arm's length SR&ED contract amounts added back at 80% when paid).
5.3 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed and the Cloud Computing Audit Rule

Under the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy (ITR paragraph 2900(2)(a) and ITA subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V)), an item qualifies as a material for SR&ED only if it is physical and tangible (in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state) and, at a given moment in the SR&ED process, composes the body of a thing on which the SR&ED is being performed. Materials can be purchased from Canadian or foreign suppliers, but their laid-down cost can only be claimed in the taxation year in which the material is actually consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada.
The CRA distinguishes between two lines on Form T661:

items: Materials Consumed (Line 320): Materials that are destroyed or rendered virtually valueless—retaining 10% or less of their original value—as a result of the SR&ED (e.g., chemicals, seed, agar, growth media, animal feed, process water entering as a feed input, or endothermic reaction energy in metallurgical/chemical refining). If 90% or more of the cost of a material is consumed in SR&ED, 100% of its cost is allowable on Line 320, and no ITC recapture applies unless scrap or insurance proceeds exceed 10% of cost.

Materials Transformed (Line 325): Materials changed or incorporated into another material, prototype, or experimental production unit that retains value greater than 10% of its original cost to the claimant or another party. While 100% claimable under both the Traditional and Proxy methods when transformed, if the resulting prototype, custom asset, or experimental product is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use, ITC Recapture under subsections 127(27) to (36) claws back the ITC earned on the transformed materials.

body.text: Where SR&ED takes place during commercial production runs (SR&ED During Production Runs Policy) or while developing a commercial asset, pilot plant, or prototype (SR&ED while Developing an Asset Policy), claimants must distinguish between Experimental Production (ED+EP)—where materials consumed or transformed up to the exact quantity needed to validate the experiment qualify—and Experimental Development Simultaneous with Commercial Production (ED+CP), where only incremental material and labour costs above standard commercial production costs qualify. Where apportioning costs between SR&ED and commercial asset construction is impracticable, the CRA's Alternative Approach estimates allowable SR&ED expenditures as total actual asset development costs minus the estimated standard costs of constructing the asset had the technology already existed.
Audit Alert: Lab Supplies, Utilities, and Cloud Computing (AWS / Azure / GCP)

Items consumed during R&D that never compose the physical body of a thing being researched—such as petri dishes, beakers, flasks, pipettes, cleaning supplies, lubricants, CDs/DVDs, and general facility utilities—do not qualify as materials on Lines 320 or 325; they are covered by the 55% PPA under the Proxy Method and can only be claimed as overhead on Line 360 if the claimant elects the Traditional Method.

In the software and artificial intelligence sectors, some startup advisory blogs suggest claiming cloud computing costs (such as AWS, GCP, or Azure staging and test environments) as "materials consumed". However, under the CRA's authoritative Materials for SR&ED Policy—which strictly requires materials to be physical, tangible matter in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state composing the body of a thing—and as confirmed by specialist R&D tax analyses, cloud computing subscriptions are intangible overhead or utility services, not physical materials. Under the Proxy Method, standard cloud subscriptions are encompassed within the 55% PPA (unless structured after December 15, 2024 as an eligible equipment lease for the right to use dedicated physical hardware that would be capital property if owned by the claimant under the SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy, or as an arm's length SR&ED contract with a Canadian taxable supplier). Under the Traditional Method, cloud computing costs segmented specifically for R&D experimentation (excluding commercial production workloads) are claimable as directly related and incremental overhead on Line 360. Furthermore, if a software or AI company purchases or leases its own dedicated high-performance computing (HPC) or GPU server hardware after December 15, 2024 for SR&ED in Canada, those hardware outlays qualify under the reinstated capital expenditure and equipment lease rules enacted by Bill C-15.

Similarly, when a claimant purchases goods, non-SR&ED services, or capital property from a non-arm's length supplier under subsection 127(11.6), the qualified expenditure for ITC purposes is capped at the lesser of the cost to the claimant and the adjusted selling cost to the non-arm's length supplier, eliminating intercompany profit.
5.5 Reinstated Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and Recapture Rules (Post-December 15, 2024)

Between January 1, 2014 and December 15, 2024, capital expenditures and equipment lease costs were ineligible for SR&ED tax incentives. Enacted on March 26, 2026 via Bill C-15, and detailed in the CRA's updated SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026) and SR&ED Shared-Use Equipment Policy (May 22, 2026), capital property acquired (and available for use under subsection 37(1.2)) after December 15, 2024 qualifies under two distinct mechanisms:

First, under Wholly Qualifying SR&ED Depreciable Property (The ≥90% ASA Test), paragraph 37(1)(b) and subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(III) and (B)(III) allow 100% of the capital cost of depreciable property (excluding land, goodwill, buildings, or leasehold interests in buildings, other than prescribed special-purpose buildings) if, at the time of acquisition, the claimant intends that all or substantially all (ASA, ≥90%) of its operating time over its expected useful life will be used in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, OR ≥90% of its value will be consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. New depreciable equipment meeting the ≥90% ASA test qualifies 100% for the subsection 37(1)(b) deductible pool (in lieu of Schedule 8 CCA) AND 100% as a qualified expenditure for the 35% or 15% ITC (with the 35% ITC on capital property being 40% refundable for CCPCs). Previously used equipment acquired after December 15, 2024 can be included in the subsection 37(1)(b) deductible pool, but remains a prescribed expenditure under ITR paragraph 2902(b) and therefore earns 0% ITC. Under Section 10.3 of the SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy, computer software or software licences acquired after December 15, 2024 solely as a tool to perform SR&ED (such as CAD/engineering simulation software) with an enduring benefit beyond one year qualify as SR&ED capital expenditures (or current expenditures if the licence benefits only the current fiscal period), whereas software intended to be incorporated into a commercial product is disallowed.

Second, under Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) (The >50% Primary Use Test under Subsection 127(9)), if new depreciable equipment (excluding general-purpose office equipment or furniture) acquired after December 15, 2024 is used for both SR&ED and commercial operations—falling short of the 90% ASA threshold—it qualifies as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) if it is used primarily (more than 50%) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada. A claimant adds 25% of the capital cost to qualified SR&ED expenditures as First-Term SUE at the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months after the equipment was acquired and became available for use, and adds a second 25% of the capital cost (totalling 50% across both terms) as Second-Term SUE in the following taxation year (at least 24 months after acquisition), provided primary SR&ED use continues.

Third, under ITC Recapture and CCA Recapture on Disposition or Commercial Conversion (Subsections 127(27) to 127(36)), if property for which an SR&ED ITC was claimed (transformed materials, prototypes, contract property, ASA capital equipment, SUE, or post-November 4, 2026 protected IP) is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use, the claimant must add ITC Recapture directly to its Part I tax payable for that year. The recaptured ITC equals the lesser of: (1) the historical SR&ED ITC earned on the property; and (2) the historical ITC percentage multiplied by the proceeds of disposition (if sold at arm's length) or the fair market value of the property at the time of disposition or conversion. Concurrently, for capital property deducted under paragraph 37(1)(b), the proceeds of disposition up to the undeducted pool balance reduce the subsection 37(1) pool on Form T661 Line 440, and any excess proceeds up to the original capital cost are included in taxable income as CCA recapture on Schedule T2SCH1.
6. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes
6.1 Jurisdictional Overview and the Federal Government Assistance "Grind"

In addition to the federal SR&ED program, nine Canadian provinces and one territory (Yukon) provide supplementary corporate (and in Newfoundland and Labrador and Yukon, individual) R&D tax credits. Three Canadian jurisdictions—Prince Edward Island (PEI), the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut—do not offer a provincial or territorial R&D tax credit.

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(9) of the federal Income Tax Act, every dollar of provincial or territorial R&D tax credit earned (whether refunded in cash or credited against provincial tax payable) is legally classified as "government assistance". Consequently, provincial R&D tax credits must be deducted on Line 513 of federal Form T661, reducing both the federal subsection 37(1) deductible pool and the federal qualified SR&ED expenditure base before the federal 35% or 15% ITC rate is applied:
Federal SR&ED ITC = (Qualified SR&ED Expenditures − Provincial R&D Tax Credits) × 35% (or 15%)

Furthermore, if a claimant uses the 55% Proxy Method, the portion of a provincial R&D tax credit that relates to the notional PPA reduces federal qualified expenditures and is included in taxable income on Schedule 1 in the year received. Because a non-refundable provincial tax credit reduces the refundable 35% federal ITC immediately in the year earned—even if the claimant owes zero provincial tax—Ontario, British Columbia, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Nova Scotia permit corporations to formally waive or renounce their non-refundable provincial R&D credit (typically on or before 6 months after the corporation's taxation year-end for federal purposes) to avoid grinding their 35% federal cash refund.

body.text: 6.3 Deep-Dive Jurisdictional Analyses
6.3.1 Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC Stacking Mechanics

Ontario corporations maintaining a permanent establishment in Ontario (as defined under ITR section 400) can stack three provincial R&D tax credits under Ontario's Taxation Act, 2007 with the federal SR&ED credit. In calculating combined entitlements, claimants must follow a strict three-step statutory ordering: first, the 8% refundable OITC (Schedule 566, up to the $3,000,000 expenditure limit) is computed on qualified Ontario expenditures. Second, because the OITC is treated as government assistance for the 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC (Schedule 508), the OITC amount is subtracted from the Ontario expenditure base before applying the 3.5% ORDTC rate (yielding an effective ORDTC rate of 3.22% and a combined Ontario credit rate of 11.22% on the first $3,000,000 of spend). Third, both the OITC and the ORDTC (unless the ORDTC is formally waived in writing within 6 months of taxation year-end) reduce the federal qualified expenditure pool on Line 513 of Form T661 before the 35% or 15% federal ITC is calculated.
For a qualifying Ontario CCPC incurring $1,000,000 in qualified current SR&ED expenditures in Ontario, the stacking arithmetic proceeds as follows:

items: Ontario OITC (8% Refundable, Schedule 566): $1,000,000 × 8% = $80,000 cash refund.
Ontario ORDTC (3.5% Non-Refundable, Schedule 508): ($1,000,000 − $80,000) = $920,000 × 3.5% = $32,200 non-refundable credit against Ontario corporate tax.
Federal SR&ED ITC (35% Refundable, Schedule T2SCH31): ($1,000,000 − $80,000 − $32,200) = $887,800 × 35% = $310,730 cash refund.

Total Combined Credits: $80,000 + $32,200 + $310,730 = $422,930 (42.293% total recovery, comprising $390,730 in cash refunds and $32,200 in non-refundable Ontario tax offset). (If the CCPC is in a tax-loss position and waives the $32,200 non-refundable ORDTC, its federal base remains $920,000, earning $920,000 × 35% = $322,000 federal cash plus $80,000 OITC = $402,000 [40.20%] in immediate cash refunds.)

6.3.2 Québec: The CRIC Regime, DCI Nexus Reform, and CDAEIA Transition (2025–2026)

Introduced in the March 25, 2025 Québec Budget (Québec Finance Bulletin 2025-6) and detailed in Revenu Québec's July 9, 2025 tax news and official government guidance, the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) applies to taxation years (or partnership fiscal periods) beginning after March 25, 2025. CRIC consolidated and eliminated Québec's legacy R&D tax measures—specifically the tax credit for salaries and wages of researchers, the tax credit for university research or public research centres, the tax credit for fees and dues paid to a research consortium, the tax credit for private partnership pre-competitive research, the tax credit for technological adaptation services, the industrial design component of the design tax credit (while retaining fashion design), and the tax holiday for foreign researchers and experts (legacy credits remain claimable only for taxation years beginning before March 26, 2025).
CRIC introduces four structural shifts for Québec claimants filing Form RD-1029.8.CR-T:

items: Size-Neutral 30% / 20% Refundable Rates: Regardless of the corporation's asset size or CCPC status, CRIC pays a 30% fully refundable tax credit on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures exceeding the applicable exclusion threshold, and a 20% fully refundable tax credit on all qualified expenditures above that $1,000,000 tranche.

Expanded Scope to Pre-Commercialization and Capital Property (CAPEX): Alongside core R&D (harmonized with federal subsection 248(1) and scientifically reviewed by the CRA), CRIC covers pre-commercialization activities that are a continuation of R&D carried out in Québec—specifically regulatory approval and certification testing/validation studies, product design (form, aesthetics, functionality improvements, and choice of materials), and quality control system implementation required for initial certification. Qualified expenditures include 100% of employee salaries, 100% of capital property/equipment acquisition costs (excluding land, buildings, or rights to use land/buildings, and subject to a special recovery tax if the property ceases to be used solely in Québec for eligible activities within 730 consecutive days), 50% of Québec subcontractor payments, and 50% of payments to eligible Québec universities, public research centres, or research consortia.

Modified Exclusion Threshold Formula: For a taxation year, gross qualified expenditures are reduced by an Exclusion Threshold equal to the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the R&D employees threshold and pre-commercialization employees threshold (calculated using the basic personal amount under the Québec personal income tax system—$18,571 for 2025—prorated by the percentage of time each employee spent on eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities).

Interaction with DCI, C3i, and the Reformed CDAEIA: For taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, Québec's Deduction for Commercialization of Innovations (DCI) (patent box) nexus ratio takes into account R&D expenditures eligible for CRIC without reducing them by the CRIC exclusion threshold, while excluding pre-commercialization expenditures. An expenditure claimed under CRIC cannot be combined with another Québec tax credit such as the C3i investment tax credit (and Québec also reinstated 100% accelerated depreciation until 2029 for M&P equipment, clean energy equipment, and zero-emission vehicles). Concurrently, for taxation years beginning after December 31, 2025, Québec reformed its 30% Tax Credit for the Development of E-Business (CDAE / TCEB) into the CDAEIA—refocusing eligibility on e-businesses that meaningfully integrate artificial intelligence (AI) functionalities (including data processing and hosting, while excluding maintenance and scaling), halving the credit when ≥50% of gross revenue comes from an application developed for use exclusively outside Québec by a related entity, and shifting the 30% total rate from 23% refundable / 7% non-refundable in 2025 to 22% refundable / 8% non-refundable in 2026, 21% / 9% in 2027, and 20% refundable / 10% non-refundable in 2028 and subsequent years.

body.text: 6.3.3 Alberta: The IEG Two-Tier Baseline and Line 557 Capital Exclusion

Alberta's Innovation Employment Grant (IEG)—enacted effective January 1, 2021 under Division 7 of Part 6 (sections 26.95 to 26.99) of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act and claimed on AT1 Schedule 29 (Form AT29) and Form AT4970—rewards incremental R&D growth on up to $4,000,000 of annual Alberta expenditures. The IEG provides an 8% refundable base payment on eligible spending up to the corporation's base level of spending (defined as the corporation's average eligible Alberta R&D spending over the two immediately preceding taxation years) plus an additional 12% incremental payment—producing a 20% combined refundable rate—on eligible spending exceeding that two-year average baseline:
IEG = (8% × Eligible Spending up to Base Level) + (20% × Eligible Spending Above Base Level)

The resulting grant is then multiplied by the taxable capital phase-out factor on Schedule 29 Line 128, which phases out linearly between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 of prior-year federal taxable capital employed in Canada (from federal Schedule T2SCH33 Line 690). For example, if a non-associated corporation with under $10,000,000 in taxable capital incurred $1,200,000 of Alberta R&D in Year 1 and $1,800,000 in Year 2 (a two-year average baseline of $1,500,000), and spends $3,000,000 in Year 3, the first $1,500,000 earns 8% ($120,000) and the incremental $1,500,000 earns 20% ($300,000), yielding a $420,000 refundable IEG. Startup corporations with $0 Alberta R&D spending in the prior two years have a $0 baseline and earn the full 20% refundable rate on up to $4,000,000 of eligible spending (up to $800,000 maximum credit).

Crucially, per Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration's June 30, 2026 update to AT1 Schedule 29, while taxation years ending before December 16, 2024 used federal Form T661 Line 559, taxation years ending after December 15, 2024 must use federal Form T661 Line 557 (current SR&ED expenditures)—meaning Alberta did not adopt the federal restoration of capital expenditures for IEG purposes. While the CRA's provincial summary page notes that the statutory Alberta deadline for Schedule 29 is 15 months after the corporation's filing-due date, practitioner guides emphasize that because Alberta relies on the CRA's verification of federal Form T661 before disbursing the IEG, claimants must meet the strict 18-month federal SR&ED filing deadline.
7. Federal Grant Ecosystem, Concessional Loans, and Assistance Stacking Mechanics
7.1 Statutory Rules on Government Assistance, Non-Government Assistance, and Contract Payments

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsections 127(9), 127(18), and 127(19) of the Income Tax Act, and the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, all government assistance, non-government assistance (under paragraph 12(1)(x)), and contract payments that a claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before its income tax return filing-due date must be deducted from both the subsection 37(1) pool and qualified SR&ED expenditures on Form T661 (Lines 513–517). If assistance and contract payments for a project exceed the SR&ED expenditures on that project, subsection 127(19) reduces the qualified expenditures of the claimant and any non-arm's length party on that project to nil, and non-arm's length parties may allocate assistance using Form T1145 under subsection 127(20).
The CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy distinguishes three categories of reductions:

items: Government Assistance (Subsection 127(9)): Assistance from a government, municipality, or other public authority (including Crown corporations, foreign governments, and government-funded non-profits) in the form of a grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax (including provincial R&D tax credits), investment allowance, or any other form of assistance, excluding the federal SR&ED ITC itself and "excluded loans" under subsection 12(11).
Non-Government Assistance (Subsection 127(9) & Paragraph 12(1)(x)): Any inducement, reimbursement, contribution, or allowance received from a private entity toward the cost of property or an expense.

Contract Payments (Subsection 127(9)): An amount paid or payable to a claimant by an arm's length taxable supplier—or by a Canadian government, municipality, public authority, or tax-exempt entity under section 149—for SR&ED to be performed for it or on its behalf. Under ITR section 4606, amounts received from the Canadian Commercial Corporation (CCC) in respect of payments received by it from foreign governments or public authorities are prescribed amounts and are exempt from reducing the performer's SR&ED claim as a contract payment. Similarly, under Com Dev Ltd. v. The Queen (99 D.T.C. 1175), fixed-price commercial supply contracts where the vendor bears the financial and technical risk to deliver a commercial product are ordinary business revenue, not SR&ED contract payments.

body.text: 7.2 Stacking NRC IRAP with SR&ED: The Proxy Overhead Leverage Effect

The National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP) is Canada's flagship direct R&D contribution program for incorporated, profit-oriented Canadian SMEs with 500 or fewer full-time equivalent (FTE) employees. Unlike SR&ED (which is a retrospective tax credit claimed with the corporate tax return), IRAP is a discretionary, advisor-led, non-repayable contribution negotiated before work begins through one of more than 250 Industrial Technology Advisors (ITAs) across Canada. While IRAP service standards cover contributions up to $10,000,000, industry data indicates that first-time awards typically range from $75,000 to $200,000 (with a median around $75,000), reimbursing 60% to 80% of internal technical salaries and up to 50% of subcontractor costs on a monthly basis. (Federal Budget 2026 also proposed $298,000,000 over three years starting in 2027–2028 to renew NRC IRAP's Clean Technology initiative.)

When stacking NRC IRAP and SR&ED on the same R&D project, claimants benefit from a critical interaction under the Income Tax Regulations: while the IRAP grant must be deducted dollar-for-dollar as federal government assistance in Part 4 of Form T661 (Line 515) when computing net qualified SR&ED expenditures, IRAP assistance does NOT reduce the salary base in Part 5 of Form T661 (ITR subsection 2900(4)) used to calculate the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA). Because IRAP only reimburses direct salaries and subcontractors and never covers overhead, the claimant earns the full 55% PPA on 100% of the gross eligible SR&ED salaries—including the salary portion reimbursed by IRAP.

7.3 Transition from the Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF) to the Strategic Response Fund (SRF)

For large-scale industrial R&D and capital deployment projects, Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED) replaced the Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF) (which operated from 2017 to 2025 across five streams) on September 5, 2025 with the $5 billion Strategic Response Fund (SRF). The SRF retains SIF's core project scale gates—requiring a minimum total eligible project cost of $20,000,000 and a minimum federal contribution of $10,000,000 (cost-sharing up to roughly 50% of eligible costs via a mix of non-repayable grants for R&D or tariff resilience and unconditionally or contingently repayable contributions for commercial scale-up)—while refocusing investments across three priority pillars: (1) Tariff Relief (Canada Strong Diversification Fund) for trade-exposed industries (steel, aluminum, automotive, forest products); (2) Large-Scale Innovation & R&D in advanced manufacturing, cleantech, critical minerals, defence/dual-use, semiconductors, biomanufacturing/life sciences, and aerospace; and (3) the AI Compute Challenge. Any project costs reimbursed through a non-repayable or forgivable SRF contribution constitute government assistance for SR&ED purposes and proportionally reduce the SR&ED expenditure base (subject to a 75% overall government assistance stacking cap), making it essential to segregate SRF capital/facility cost buckets from SR&ED experimental development labour buckets at the outset.
7.4 Concessional Loans and the Bill C-69 Reversal of CAE Inc. v. The Queen

In CAE Inc. v. The Queen (2021 TCC / 2022 FCA; leave to appeal dismissed by the Supreme Court of Canada in May 2023), the courts ruled that the entire $250,000,000 principal of a below-market (2.5% interest) unconditionally repayable loan received by CAE Inc. under Industry Canada's Strategic Aerospace and Defence Initiative (SADI) constituted "government assistance" under subsection 127(9), disqualifying $250,000,000 of CAE's $700,000,000 SR&ED expenditure pool. That ruling threatened Canadian companies receiving low- or zero-interest loans from ISED (SIF/SRF), Regional Development Agencies, the Business Development Bank of Canada (BDC), Export Development Canada (EDC), the Canada Infrastructure Bank (CIB), or Farm Credit Canada (FCC).

To reverse CAE Inc., Parliament enacted Bill C-69 (Budget Implementation Act, 2024, No. 1) on June 20, 2024, with retroactive effect to January 1, 2020 (applying to loans made after 2019). Bill C-69 amended subsection 127(9) and added subparagraph 12(1)(x)(ix) and the definition of "excluded loan" in subsection 12(11) of the ITA. Under subsection 12(11), a loan is an "excluded loan"—and is therefore completely exempt from reducing SR&ED expenditures or triggering an income inclusion—if it meets four conditions: (1) it is a non-forgivable loan evidenced in writing; (2) it is provided by a government, municipality, or other public authority in Canada (or by a Canadian resident or partnership that would not have made the loan but for the receipt of amounts from a public authority); (3) bona fide arrangements for repayment of the loan within a reasonable time were made at the time the loan was granted; and (4) the funds are used for the purpose of earning income from a business or property.
