8.2 Pre-Claim Approval (Launched April 1, 2026), FTCAS, and SALT
To provide upfront certainty to innovators and accelerate refund processing, the CRA administers three pre-filing and advisory mechanisms:

items: Elective Pre-Claim Approval (Launched April 1, 2026): Detailed in the 2026 Spring Economic Update and CRA guidance, eligible businesses with under $25,000,000 in gross business income can apply for formal Pre-Claim Approval before filing their tax return through a four-step, 8-week process. In Step 1, the business opens a pre-claim approval request on Canada.ca (existing claimants in good standing receive a case number in My Business Account within 2 business days; new claimants are contacted by phone within 5 business days). In Step 2, the business submits its application and documents in My Business Account. In Step 3, within 4 weeks of submission, a 2-to-5-hour virtual or in-person meeting with a CRA SR&ED specialist takes place (mandatory for new claimants; optional/as-needed for existing claimants in good standing). In Step 4, within 8 weeks of submission, the CRA issues its pre-claim approval determination, which remains valid for up to 3 years. When the claimant subsequently files its tax return, if the pre-approved claim requires an expenditure review, the CRA's processing service standard is cut in half from 180 calendar days to 90 calendar days.

First-Time Claimant Advisory Service (FTCAS): A post-filing educational service (not an audit) where CRA officials meet virtually with selected first-time SR&ED claimants to review project scoping, documentation standards, and cost-allocation methodologies for future claims. Claimants cannot request FTCAS on demand; the CRA selects participants, and participation is mandatory if selected.

Self-Assessment and Learning Tool (SALT): An online diagnostic questionnaire provided on Canada.ca allowing businesses to self-evaluate whether their projects satisfy the "Why" and "How" requirements and estimate potential ITCs prior to claiming.

body.text: 8.3 The CRA Technical and Financial Review Process, Service Standards, and Dispute Resolution

When an SR&ED claim is filed, it undergoes automated risk assessment (augmented by CRA analytics and AI screening in 2026). Unreviewed refundable claims are typically processed within 60 to 120 calendar days. If a claim is selected for a technical and financial review, the CRA's published service standard is 180 calendar days from receipt of a complete claim for refundable claims (and 90 calendar days for pre-approved expenditure-only reviews; non-refundable claims have no fixed service standard).

Under the CRA's The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (updated April 20, 2026), a selected claim cannot be withdrawn by the taxpayer because the Part 10 certification on Form T661 is irrevocable. The review is conducted jointly by a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA)—a scientist or engineer reporting to a Research and Technology Manager (RTM) who evaluates technical eligibility under subsection 248(1), conducts virtual or on-site interviews and facility tours with R&D staff, examines contemporaneous evidence (Form T661 Lines 270–282), and prepares the SR&ED Project Eligibility Report—and a Financial Reviewer (FR), a tax auditor reporting to a Financial Review Manager (FRM) who audits payroll T4s, time-tracking allocations, contracts, general ledger accounts, unpaid amounts, and government assistance.

If adjustments are proposed, the CRA sends a formal Proposal Package containing the SR&ED Project Eligibility Report and financial adjustment schedules, giving the claimant 30 calendar days to submit written representations and additional factual evidence. If concerns remain unresolved, the claimant follows the CRA's three-step Dispute Resolution process: (1) Talk with the RTA/FR; (2) Escalate to the RTM/FRM; and (3) Request an Administrative Review (which evaluates whether the review complied with SR&ED legislation, policy, and due process, rather than performing a second technical review). Once a Notice of Assessment or Reassessment is issued, the claimant may file a formal Notice of Objection with the CRA Appeals Branch (historically within 90 days; Federal Budget 2026 proposed extending the objection deadline for most taxpayers from 90 days to one year after the mailing of the Notice of Assessment), followed by an appeal to the Tax Court of Canada.
8.4 Penalties: Part 9 Claim Preparer Penalty and Subsection 163(2) Gross Negligence Penalties

First, under Part 9 of Form T661 (Claim Preparer Information), claimants must disclose every external claim preparer who accepted consideration to prepare or assist in preparing the SR&ED claim, including their billing arrangement (contingency percentage, flat fee, or hourly rate). If no claim preparer was involved, the claimant must still complete lines 935, 970, and 975. If Part 9 information is missing, incomplete, or inaccurate, a $1,000 penalty may be assessed for which the claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally (or solidarily) liable, although a Part 9 deficiency does not invalidate the SR&ED claim itself. (Note: Federal Budget 2026 also proposed broad inflation adjustments to fixed-dollar administrative penalties across the ITA, alongside a 3× multiplier for medium corporations [$10M–$50M taxable capital] and an 8× multiplier for large corporations [>$50M taxable capital] starting for taxation years beginning on or after January 1, 2027.)

Second, under the CRA's Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (updated January 28, 2025; subsection 163(2), paragraphs 163(2)(a) and (d), and subsection 163(2.1) of the ITA), if the CRA establishes on a balance of probabilities (subsection 163(3)) that a claimant knowingly, or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence, made or participated in a false statement or omission on an original or amended SR&ED claim, a civil penalty applies equal to the greater of $100 or 50% of the sum of: (1) the understated Part I tax payable reasonably attributable to the false statement or omission (paragraph 163(2)(a), with overstated pool deductions and overstated ITCs deemed deducted first, and net losses deemed not less than zero under subsection 163(2.1)); plus (2) the refund of the overstated refundable ITC claimed by the claimant (paragraph 163(2)(d)), resulting in a direct 50% penalty on the disallowed cash refund even where no Part I tax is payable. In cases of criminal fraud or third-party promoter misrepresentation, fines of 150% to 300% of the claimed credits have been imposed (R v. Elhami, 2017 QCCQ 2684; Tempora, SCC 2018).
9. Landmark and Contemporary SR&ED Jurisprudence (1989–2026)

Canadian SR&ED law is heavily shaped by decisions of the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) and the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA). Even after the CRA introduced its simplified "Why" and "How" administrative guidelines in August 2021, both the TCC and FCA have repeatedly ruled that the Five Questions of Northwest Hydraulic remain the binding legal test for interpreting subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act.
9.1 Comprehensive Case Law Digest: Technological Eligibility and Financial Precedents

cells: Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 D.T.C. 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520

Landmark Precedent: Justice Bowman formulated the Five Questions test. Established the doctrine of "system uncertainty" (technological uncertainty can arise from the unpredictable interaction of known components integrated into a complex system) and defined the boundary between experimental development and routine engineering.

Endorsed Northwest Hydraulic at the appellate level. Held that scientific research requires repeatability and verifiability supported by contemporaneous test data; obtaining a patent or final prototype alone does not prove systematic investigation (though Round 2 showed judicial sympathy where the lead engineer died prior to trial).
Rainbow Pipe Line Co. v. The Queen, 99 D.T.C. 1081

Held that technological advancement does not require project success: conclusively proving through systematic testing that a hypothesized technical solution does not work eliminates a plausible option and constitutes an advancement in technological knowledge.
Consoltex Inc. v. The Queen, 97 D.T.C. 724 & Les Cultures Laflamme, 89-2514(IT)
Textile manufacturing & agriculture / commercial sale of trials

Held that subsequent commercial sale of experimental production or transformed materials does not retroactively invalidate genuine SR&ED performed during development. (Prompted Parliament to enact the ITC Recapture rules in subsections 127(27)–(36) to claw back material/asset ITCs upon sale without disqualifying SR&ED labour).
Com Dev Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 D.T.C. 1175

Distinguished a commercial fixed-price supply contract (where the manufacturer bears technical and financial overrun risk to deliver a product) from a "contract payment" for SR&ED performed on behalf of a government or customer.
HSC Research Development Corp. (1995), Mindready Solutions (2015 CCI 17), & CO2 Solution Technologies (2019 CCI 286)

Established the legal criteria for de facto control by public corporations or non-residents under subsection 256(5.1), which disqualifies a private company from CCPC status (though for tax years beginning after Dec 15, 2024, Eligible Canadian Public Corporations now qualify for the 35% refundable rate under Bill C-15).
Easyway Cattle Co. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 211 & Westsource Group, 2017 TCC 9

Strictly enforced the 18-month statutory reporting deadline: failing to file Schedule T2SCH31 or filing project details only under a related corporation's return before the 18-month bar is fatal to earning ITCs.
Béton Mobile du Québec Inc. v. The Queen, 2019 CCI 278

Justice Lafleur allowed 6 projects where the taxpayer proved a structured two-stage methodology (controlled laboratory plastic/hard-state testing followed by mobile mixer calibration trials) to resolve multi-variable binder/additive interactions, while denying 8 projects lacking systematic hypothesis testing.
National R&D Inc. v. The Queen, 2020 TCC 47 (aff'd 2022 FCA; SCC leave denied) & Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen, 2021 FCA 88 (aff'g 2019 TCC 246)
Software (automated SR&ED SQL tool) & Metal stamping

Taxpayers argued that because the words "scientific method" do not appear in subsection 248(1), Criterion 3 of Northwest Hydraulic was unlawful. The FCA flatly rejected this, holding that "systematic investigation or search... by means of experiment or analysis" mandates the discipline of the scientific method, logical progression from premise to result, and contemporaneous records.
CAE Inc. v. The Queen, 2021 TCC / 2022 FCA (SCC leave denied May 2023)
Aerospace flight simulators / Low-interest government loans

Ruled that a $250M below-market (2.5%) federal SADI loan constituted "government assistance" under s. 127(9), disqualifying $250M of R&D spend. Legislatively reversed by Bill C-69 (enacted June 20, 2024, retroactive to Jan 1, 2020) via s. 12(11) "excluded loans".
Airzone One Ltd. v. The Queen, 2022 TCC

Formally mapped the CRA's 2021 "Why" and "How" guidelines to Northwest Hydraulic: Questions 1 and 4 correspond to the "Why" (uncertainty and advancement), while Questions 2, 3, and 5 correspond to the "How" (hypotheses, systematic testing, and contemporaneous records).
JEC Distributors Inc. v. The King, 2022 TCC 170 & Mold Leaders Inc. v. The King, 2023 TCC / 2024 FCA
Automotive resistance welding sensors & Hard-milling W360 steel

Confirmed that technological uncertainty is an objective industry standard, not a subjective company standard: proving that the claimant's own technicians did not know how to solve electrical noise or machine harder W360 steel fails without evidence that the problem exceeded standard practice known to competent engineers/metallurgists in the field.
Canafric Inc. v. The King, 2023 TCC & Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. The King, 2025 TCC
Food science / shelf-stable beverage & culinary formulations

In Manning Canning, Justice Bodie held that: (1) technological uncertainty can exist even where known ingredients/preservatives exist publicly, provided they have never been combined in that specific context (shelf-stable room-temperature vinegar beverage); and (2) contemporaneous records need only track hypotheses, tests, and measurable metrics (pH, microbial counts) for someone skilled in the field, not be written as a textbook for a layperson.
Cloud SaaS / React & Redux architecture integration

Landmark software victory confirming that systemic uncertainty in integrating open-source frameworks (React/Redux performance bottlenecks) qualifies as SR&ED when investigated holistically through systematic hypothesis testing beyond routine debugging.
Les Éléments Chauffants Tempora Inc. v. The King, 2025 TCC 173

Held that plagiarizing supplier and website text into Form T661 technical narratives constituted a misrepresentation attributable to neglect or carelessness under ITA subparagraph 152(4)(a)(i), allowing the CRA to reopen statute-barred taxation years and deny the claims.
Vortex Energy Services Ltd. v. The King, 2025 TCC 63 & Tuna Temple Inc. v. The King, 2025 TCC 183
Fracking water heaters & Food processing (13 projects)
Rejected trial-and-error prototyping, vague post-hoc hypotheses, and unsubstantiated wage allocations split evenly across production batches without contemporaneous time records.
Willowglen Systems Inc. v. The King, 2026 TCC 7
Industrial SCADA software vs. SIL 4 train-control system

Illustrated the exact software SR&ED boundary in 2026: allowed the SIL 4 train-control project due to genuine cumulative "system uncertainty" unresolvable by available methods, but disallowed $1,293,692 on the SCADACOM-5 project because modernizing and scaling up legacy software using known tools is commercial product development, not experimental development.

body.text: 10. Comprehensive Audit Readiness Checklist for Canadian R&D Claimants

To ensure full statutory compliance across federal and provincial audits in 2026 and beyond, corporate tax directors, CFOs, and R&D leads should verify eight mandatory audit controls before submitting Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31:

items: Project-Level Scoping ("Why" and "How" Alignment): Frame every Part 2 project narrative on Form T661 around the specific technological uncertainty (distinguishing objective industry knowledge limits from routine engineering, as required by Willowglen Systems [2026 TCC 7] and JEC Distributors [2022 TCC 170]) and never copy vendor or website text into project narratives (Tempora [2025 TCC 173]).

Contemporaneous Technical Evidence (Form T661 Lines 270–282): Maintain dated artefacts created during the experimentation—Git commit logs linked to experimental branches, architecture decision records, test bench spreadsheets with numerical parameters, failed prototype logs, and dated lab notes (Manning Canning [2025 TCC]; Dazzm Inc. [2024 TCC 129]; Mac & Mac Hydrodemolition).

Time-Tracking and Payroll Substantiation: Substantiate employee SR&ED percentages with contemporaneous time sheets, Jira/sprint tickets, or engineering project calendars—particularly for any employee allocated above 80% to SR&ED (Tuna Temple [2025 TCC 183]). Verify that specified employees' bonuses and profit-based remuneration are stripped from Line 305 and Line 812, apply the 2026 YMPE ($74,600) caps ($373,000 on Line 305; lesser of 75% salary or $186,500 on Line 858), and file Form T1174 if shared across associated corporations.

180-Day Unpaid Amounts Reconciliation (Subsections 78(4) and 127(26)): Reconcile year-end accrued bonuses, salaries, and subcontractor/material payables against actual cash disbursements made within 180 days after fiscal year-end, reporting unpaid wages on Line 315 and other unpaid current costs on Line 520.

Post-December 15, 2024 Capital Expenditure & Lease Segregation (Bill C-15): For depreciable equipment acquired or leased on or after December 16, 2024, document the acquisition/available-for-use date and log SR&ED operating time percentages to substantiate either the ≥90% ASA test (100% inclusion) or the >50% primary use test for Shared-Use Equipment (25%/25% SUE inclusion) and Proxy Method equipment leases (50% inclusion on Line 355). Remember to exclude reinstated federal capital expenditures from the Alberta IEG calculation (using Form T661 Line 557 on AT1 Schedule 29).

Subcontractor & Taxable Supplier Verification: Confirm that all arm's length contractors claimed on Line 340 performed the SR&ED physically in Canada, are Canadian taxable suppliers, and have statements of work and contracts on file; ensure non-arm's length contracts are reported on Line 345 and supported by a timely filed Form T1146 if transferring qualified expenditures.

Government Assistance & Concessional Loan Review (Bill C-69): Disclose all NRC IRAP grants, non-repayable SRF/SIF contributions, and provincial R&D tax credits receivable by the filing-due date on Lines 513–515, while ensuring that bona fide non-forgivable concessional loans from public authorities (qualifying as "excluded loans" under subsection 12(11)) are not erroneously deducted from the SR&ED expenditure pool.

Strict Calendar Control on the 18-Month Statutory Bar & Part 9 Disclosure: File Form T661, Schedule T2SCH31 (or Form T2038(IND)), and all applicable provincial schedules (Schedule 566/508/568, Form RD-1029.8.CR-T, Form T666, AT1 Schedule 29, Schedule 403/380/340/360/301/442) well in advance of the non-extendable 18-month corporate reporting deadline, and verify that Part 9 (Claim Preparer Information) and Part 10 (Certification) of Form T661 are completely and accurately populated.
